preamble.summary: Ben Sira presents a theological defense of medicine: the physician's art comes from God, and the wise man does not reject it. Instructions for mourning follow, balanced by counsel against excessive grief. The chapter concludes with a vivid portrait of manual laborers -- the farmer, the engraver, the smith, and the potter -- who sustain the fabric of society but do not sit in the council of rulers.
preamble.remarkable: The command 'Honor the physician' (v. 1) became one of the most cited verses in the history of medical ethics and was foundational for medieval Christian and Jewish attitudes toward medicine. The portrait of craftsmen (vv. 25-39) is the most detailed description of ancient trades in any biblical or deuterocanonical text and provides invaluable social-historical data.
preamble.friction: The concluding contrast between manual laborers and the scribe (continued in chapter 39) has been criticized as elitist. Ben Sira clearly values the scribe's vocation above manual trades, though he acknowledges that craftsmen are indispensable to civilization.
preamble.connections: Exodus 15:26 (the Lord your healer); 2 Chronicles 16:12 (Asa criticized for consulting physicians instead of God); Genesis 50:2 (Joseph commands physicians to embalm Jacob); Proverbs 31:10-31 (domestic industry).

verses.text_latin: Honora medicum propter necessitatem etenim illum creavit Altissimus.
verses.rendering: Honor the physician for his service, for the Most High created him.
translator_notes: One of the most influential verses in all deuterocanonical literature. By grounding the physician's authority in divine creation, Ben Sira resolves the tension between faith-healing and medicine.

key_terms.note: The Greek iatros behind Jerome's medicus was a professional healer; Ben Sira legitimizes the entire medical profession as divinely ordained.

verses.text_latin: A Deo est enim omnis medella et a rege accipiet donationem.
verses.rendering: For all healing comes from God, and the physician will receive gifts from the king.
translator_notes: Healing is ultimately divine, but the physician's social status is affirmed: he receives patronage from the highest authority.

key_terms.note: A poetic term for cure or remedy, emphasizing the restorative process rather than the technique employed.

verses.text_latin: Disciplina medici exaltabit caput illius et in conspectu magnatorum conlaudabitur.
verses.rendering: The skill of the physician lifts his head high, and in the presence of the great he is admired.

key_terms.note: Disciplina encompasses both learned knowledge and practiced technique; the physician's competence is the product of rigorous training.

verses.text_latin: Altissimus creavit de terra medicamenta et vir prudens non abhorrebit illa.
verses.rendering: The Most High created medicines from the earth, and a prudent man will not despise them.
translator_notes: A decisive theological statement: pharmaceuticals derived from natural substances are part of God's creation, not pagan sorcery. This verse was repeatedly cited in medieval debates over the legitimacy of herbal medicine.

key_terms.note: Remedies derived from plants and minerals; the term covers the full range of ancient pharmacology.

verses.text_latin: Nonne a ligno indulcata est aqua amara.
verses.rendering: Was not bitter water made sweet by a piece of wood?
translator_notes: An allusion to Exodus 15:25, where Moses cast a tree into the bitter waters of Marah to make them drinkable -- a biblical precedent for using natural substances to heal.

verses.text_latin: Ad agnitionem hominum virtus illorum et dedit hominibus scientiam Altissimus honorari in mirabilibus suis.
verses.rendering: Their power is made known to mankind, and the Most High gave knowledge to mortals so that he might be glorified through his wonders.
translator_notes: Medical knowledge itself is a revelation: God grants it so that human healing becomes an occasion for divine praise.

key_terms.note: Here specifically medical and pharmacological knowledge, treated as a divine gift rather than a human invention.

verses.text_latin: In his curans mitigabit dolorem et unguentarius faciet pigmenta suavitatis et unctiones conficiet sanitatis et non consummabuntur opera eius.
verses.rendering: With these the physician soothes pain; the pharmacist prepares fragrant compounds and blends healing ointments, and his works are never finished.
translator_notes: The pharmacist (unguentarius) is distinguished from the physician -- an early recognition of pharmacy as a distinct profession.

key_terms.note: Literally 'ointment maker'; the specialist who compounds medicines, distinct from the diagnosing physician.

verses.text_latin: Pax enim Dei super faciem terrae.
verses.rendering: For the peace of God extends over the face of the earth.
translator_notes: A surprising interjection: healing arts are expressions of God's shalom -- his comprehensive well-being for creation.

key_terms.note: Not merely absence of conflict but total well-being; health and healing are manifestations of divine shalom.

verses.text_latin: Fili in tua infirmitate ne despicias te ipsum sed ora Dominum et ipse curabit te.
verses.rendering: My son, in your illness do not despair, but pray to the Lord and he will heal you.
translator_notes: Prayer comes first -- not because medicine is rejected, but because the ultimate source of healing is God. The sequence is: pray, then consult the physician.

verses.text_latin: Averte a delicto et dirige manus et ab omni delicto munda cor tuum.
verses.rendering: Turn away from sin and direct your hands aright, and cleanse your heart from every offense.
translator_notes: Moral self-examination accompanies the healing process: Ben Sira does not separate physical illness from the moral life, without simplistically equating them.

verses.text_latin: Da suavitatem et memoriam similaginis et inpingua oblationem et da locum medico.
verses.rendering: Offer sweet incense and a memorial of fine flour, and enrich the offering -- then give place to the physician.
translator_notes: The prescribed sequence: sacrifice and prayer first, then medical treatment. Both are legitimate responses to illness.

key_terms.note: A directive to make room for professional medical care after fulfilling religious obligations -- not instead of them.

verses.text_latin: Etenim illum Dominus creavit et non discedat a te quia opera eius sunt necessaria.
verses.rendering: For the Lord created him too; let him not depart from you, for his services are necessary.
translator_notes: Reaffirms v. 1: the physician's existence is divinely willed, and his work is genuinely needed -- not a concession to weak faith.

verses.text_latin: Est enim quando in manus illorum incursus.
verses.rendering: For there is a time when recovery lies in their hands.
translator_notes: A remarkably modern recognition that in certain situations, the physician's intervention is the decisive factor in survival.

key_terms.note: Literally 'an advance' or 'onset'; here meaning the turning point toward health, which sometimes depends entirely on medical skill.

verses.text_latin: Et ipsi Dominum deprecabuntur ut dirigat requiem eorum et sanitatem propter conversationem illorum.
verses.rendering: And they too will pray to the Lord, that he may grant them relief and healing for the sake of their patient's way of life.
translator_notes: The physician himself prays -- medicine and prayer are not alternatives but collaborators in the healing process.

verses.text_latin: Qui delinquit in conspectu eius qui fecit eum incidet in manus medici.
verses.rendering: He who sins before his Maker will fall into the hands of the physician.
translator_notes: A sobering warning: while medicine is legitimate, needing it may sometimes result from one's own moral failures. The verse does not condemn all illness as punishment, but acknowledges the connection between conduct and health.

verses.text_latin: Fili in mortuum produc lacrimas et quasi dira passus incipe plorare et secundum iudicium contege corpus illius et non despicias sepulturam illius.
verses.rendering: My son, shed tears over the dead, and as one who suffers terribly begin to weep; wrap the body according to custom, and do not neglect the burial.
translator_notes: The transition to mourning rituals. Proper burial and genuine grief are obligations, not optional expressions of sentiment.

key_terms.note: Proper interment was a sacred duty in ancient Israel; to leave a body unburied was the ultimate dishonor (cf. Tobit 1:17-18).

verses.text_latin: Propter delaturam autem amare fer luctum illius uno die et consolare propter tristitiam.
verses.rendering: Bear the bitter grief of mourning for one day on account of reproach, then console yourself in your sorrow.
translator_notes: Ben Sira counsels genuine but bounded mourning: grief has its proper season, but must not become self-destructive.

verses.text_latin: Et fac luctum secundum meritum eius uno die vel duobus propter detractionem.
verses.rendering: And mourn according to what is fitting, one day or two, to avoid gossip.
translator_notes: Social reputation is a practical concern: excessive public mourning may attract harmful talk.

verses.text_latin: A tristitia enim festinat mors et cooperit virtutem et tristitia cordis flectit cervicem.
verses.rendering: For grief hastens death and overwhelms one's strength; sorrow of heart bows the neck.
translator_notes: A medical observation embedded in moral advice: prolonged grief has physiological consequences.

verses.text_latin: In abductione permanet tristitia et substantia inopis secundum cor eius.
verses.rendering: In exile sorrow endures, and the life of the poor weighs on the heart.

verses.text_latin: Ne dederis in tristitia cor tuum sed repelle eam a te et memento novissimorum.
verses.rendering: Do not give your heart to sorrow, but drive it from you and remember the end.
translator_notes: 'Remember the end' -- the inevitability of one's own death, which puts mourning in perspective.

key_terms.note: The last things; one's own mortality, which relativizes present grief.

verses.text_latin: Noli oblivisci neque enim est conversio et huic nihil proderis et te ipsum pessimabis.
verses.rendering: Do not forget: there is no return. You will not help the dead, and you will only harm yourself.
translator_notes: A blunt statement of finality: the dead cannot be recalled, and excessive mourning serves no one.

key_terms.note: No turning back from death; Ben Sira's theology here does not include resurrection, reflecting pre-Maccabean thought.

verses.text_latin: Memor esto iudicii mei sic enim erit et tuum mihi heri et tibi hodie.
verses.rendering: Remember my judgment, for so too will be yours: yesterday it was mine, today it is yours.
translator_notes: The dead speak to the living: my fate will be yours. A memento mori that encourages the living to accept mortality.

verses.text_latin: In requie mortui requiescere fac memoriam eius et consolare illum in exitu spiritus sui.
verses.rendering: When the dead is at rest, let his memory rest also, and be comforted when his spirit departs.
translator_notes: Allow the dead their peace; continuing grief disturbs both the living and, symbolically, the dead.

key_terms.note: Death as rest -- a gentle metaphor that frames dying as cessation of labor rather than annihilation.

verses.text_latin: Sapientia scribae in tempore vacuitatis et qui minoratur actu sapientiam percipiet.
verses.rendering: The wisdom of the scribe depends on the leisure of study, and he who has less to do can become wise.
translator_notes: The pivotal verse that introduces the contrast between intellectual and manual labor. Wisdom requires leisure (vacuitas) -- time freed from physical toil.

key_terms.note: Not idleness but scholastic leisure: the freedom from manual labor that permits sustained intellectual and spiritual pursuit. The Greek equivalent is schole, from which 'school' derives.

verses.text_latin: Qua sapientia replebitur qui tenet aratrum et qui gloriatur in iaculo stimuli boves agit et conversatur in operibus eorum et enarratio eius in filiis taurorum.
verses.rendering: How can the one who holds the plow become wise, who takes pride in wielding the goad, who drives oxen and is occupied with their labors, and whose talk is only of young bulls?
translator_notes: The farmer is the first of four craftsmen portrayed. His absorption in agricultural work leaves no room for the study that wisdom requires.

key_terms.note: The primary instrument of ancient agriculture; holding it represents total commitment to physical labor.
A pointed stick for driving oxen; the farmer's tool becomes a metonymy for his entire vocation.

verses.text_latin: Cor suum dabit ad versandos sulcos et vigilia eius in sagina vaccarum.
verses.rendering: He sets his heart on turning furrows, and his wakeful care is for fattening heifers.

key_terms.note: The grooves cut by the plow; the farmer's mind runs in the same tracks as his field.

verses.text_latin: Sic omnis faber et architectus qui noctem tamquam diem transigit qui sculpit signacula sculptilia et adsiduitas eius variat picturam.
verses.rendering: So too every artisan and master builder who works through the night as through the day, who carves engraved seals, and whose constant effort varies the design.
translator_notes: The engraver/seal-carver: a skilled artisan whose work requires unceasing concentration and artistic sensitivity.

key_terms.note: Carved seal stones used for authenticating documents; their production required extraordinary precision and artistic skill.

verses.text_latin: Cor suum dabit in similitudinem picturae et vigilia sua perficiet opus.
verses.rendering: He sets his heart on producing a lifelike image, and his watchful labor brings the work to completion.

verses.text_latin: Sic faber ferrarius sedens iuxta incudem et considerans opus ferri vapor ignis uret carnes eius et in calore fornacis concertatur.
verses.rendering: So too the smith sitting beside the anvil, studying the iron work: the vapor of fire scorches his flesh, and he contends with the heat of the furnace.
translator_notes: The most physically vivid of the four portraits: the smith endures bodily suffering in his craft.

key_terms.note: An ironworker; the Latin specifically identifies him as working with ferrum (iron), the dominant metal of the period.
The iron block on which metal is hammered; the smith's central tool and workplace.

verses.text_latin: Vox mallei innovat aurem eius et contra similitudinem vasis oculus eius.
verses.rendering: The sound of the hammer rings ceaselessly in his ear, and his eye is fixed on the pattern of the vessel.
translator_notes: Sensory immersion: the smith's entire perceptual world is consumed by his work -- hearing the hammer, seeing the emerging form.

verses.text_latin: Cor suum dabit in consummationem operum et vigilia sua ornabit in perfectionem.
verses.rendering: He sets his heart on completing his works, and his watchful care perfects the finishing.

verses.text_latin: Sic figulus sedens ad opus suum convertens pedibus suis rotam qui in sollicitudine positus est semper super opus suum et in numero est omnis operatio eius.
verses.rendering: So too the potter sitting at his work, turning the wheel with his feet, who is always anxiously devoted to his work, and all his output is measured by number.
translator_notes: The potter is the fourth and final craftsman. The foot-operated wheel dates this description to the Hellenistic period.

key_terms.note: The clay-worker; pottery was one of the most essential and ubiquitous trades in the ancient world.
The potter's wheel, here specifically the foot-driven type that allowed both hands to shape the clay.

verses.text_latin: In brachio suo formabit lutum et ante pedes suos curvabit virtutem suam.
verses.rendering: With his arm he shapes the clay, and before his feet he bends his strength.
translator_notes: The physical posture of the potter: arms working the clay, body stooped, all strength directed into the material.

key_terms.note: The raw material of pottery; its malleability in the potter's hands became a universal metaphor for God's sovereignty over humanity (Isaiah 64:8, Romans 9:21).

verses.text_latin: Cor suum dabit ut consummet linitionem et vigilia sua mundabit fornacem.
verses.rendering: He sets his heart on finishing the glazing, and his watchful care tends the kiln.

key_terms.note: The application of a smooth coating before firing; a finishing technique that required precise timing and temperature control.
The furnace in which pottery is fired; maintaining correct temperature was crucial and required constant attention.

verses.text_latin: Omnes hi in manibus suis speraverunt et unusquisque in arte sua sapiens est.
verses.rendering: All these trust in their hands, and each is wise in his own craft.
translator_notes: Ben Sira grants genuine wisdom (sapiens) to the craftsmen within their domain -- their expertise is real, though limited in scope.

verses.text_latin: Sine his omnibus non aedificatur civitas.
verses.rendering: Without all of these, no city is built.
translator_notes: The essential dignity of manual labor: civilization itself depends on these workers. Ben Sira is not contemptuous of their contribution.

key_terms.note: The organized human community; its physical existence depends on the labor of craftsmen.

verses.text_latin: Et non inhabitabunt nec inambulabunt et in ecclesiam non transilient.
verses.rendering: Yet they will not dwell there as leaders, nor walk about in prominence, nor have a seat in the assembly.
translator_notes: The crucial distinction: craftsmen build the city but do not govern it. Ben Sira reserves civic and religious leadership for the learned scribe.

key_terms.note: The deliberative body of the community; ecclesia here denotes the council where civic and religious decisions are made.

verses.text_latin: Super sellam iudicis non sedebunt et testamentum iudicii non intelligent et non patefacient disciplinam et iudicium et in parabolis non invenientur.
verses.rendering: They will not sit on the judge's seat, nor understand the covenant of judgment; they will not expound instruction and law, nor be found among those who speak in proverbs.
translator_notes: The judicial, legal, and literary functions of wisdom are reserved for those with the leisure to study. The craftsmen's exclusion is practical, not moral.

key_terms.note: The legal and covenantal framework within which justice is administered; mastery of it requires sustained study.
The wisdom genre par excellence: mashal, the crafted comparison that distills truth into memorable form.

verses.text_latin: Sed creaturam aevi confirmabunt et deprecatio illorum in operatione artis accomodantes animam suam et conquirentes in lege Altissimi.
verses.rendering: But they sustain the fabric of the age, and their prayer is in the practice of their craft, applying their souls and seeking understanding in the law of the Most High.
translator_notes: The chapter's closing affirmation: the craftsmen's work is itself a form of prayer. Their labor sustains the world order (creaturam aevi), even if they do not articulate it in words.

key_terms.note: The created order of the present world; the craftsmen's labor maintains the physical infrastructure of civilization across time.
